case_study_insert.main_stem: Zaara Eyewear (ZAE) is a public limited company in the eyewear e-commerce sector, employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2008 by Zaara Nasser, the business sells prescription frames and sunglasses online, and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. ZAE plans to invest $960,000 in an automated lens-fitting line and a new mobile shopping platform, financed by a $600,000 share issue and a $360,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $222,000 a year, a variable cost of $18.00 a unit and a selling price of $55.00, and currently produces 18,500 units a year. ZAE faces two problems: the lens-fitting defect rate has reached 4.2% and online returns are rising as sales grow.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research Summary — Q3 2025: An online survey of 750 shoppers found 63% buy eyewear mainly online, and 49% would pay $20 more for custom-fitted frames. The web store shipped 4,600 orders last quarter with a 4.2% defect-related return rate, down from 6.8% a year earlier. Average delivery time is 3.1 days. Social-media campaign reach was 220,000 impressions with a 2.9% click-through rate, and customer satisfaction averaged 4.3 out of 5. A team working pilot in the fitting bay is under review, and HR is comparing an individual accuracy bonus with a profit sharing scheme to reduce the 4.2% defect rate.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Zaara Eyewear as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing interest on ZAE's $360,000 bank loan. (2) The national minimum wage rises 6.4% to $13.60 an hour from April 2026, affecting ZAE's workforce of 50. (3) Lens and frame input costs rose 10.5% year-on-year, while consumer spending on accessories grew 3.3% and online eyewear returns average 12%.

questions.question_text: ZAE is funding its $960,000 lens-fitting line with a $600,000 share issue and a $360,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for ZAE of using the share issue rather than a larger bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Share issue money does not require interest or repayment, so it protects ZAE's cash flow while the public limited company carries fixed costs of $222,000 a year and a 4.2% defect rate that forces remakes. With the base rate rising to 5.0%, a larger loan would add interest expense; equity avoids this, leaving more of the $55.00 selling price available to cover the 10.5% rise in lens and frame costs.

Point 2: Issuing $600,000 of shares strengthens the capital base for a public limited company without creating a lender who could threaten the $960,000 investment if cash flow weakens. It gives ZAE more financial flexibility to fund the new mobile platform and to weather the 4.2% return rate, and new shareholders may bring useful retail or technology expertise that supports growth in online eyewear without adding fixed-interest commitments, and the stronger equity base leaves room to borrow further if the $960,000 line needs extra funding.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to ZAE's costs, defects, financing mix and legal structure.

questions.question_text: ZAE wants to increase repeat orders for its frames and sunglasses. Consider a seasonal price discount, a free-delivery offer, or a loyalty scheme. Which should ZAE choose to build repeat custom? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Seasonal price discount: Cutting the $55.00 price would stimulate short-term demand and help fill the new automated line's capacity, clearing the 18,500-unit target. However, a discount comes straight out of the $37.00 contribution per unit, and with lens costs up 10.5% and a 4.2% defect rate, ZAE can ill afford to give away margin. Discounts also train customers to wait for sales rather than buy at full price.

Free-delivery offer: Removing delivery charges reduces a common barrier for the 63% of 750 surveyed shoppers who buy eyewear online and can lift conversion against a 2.9% click-through rate. It is simple to promote and supports the 3.1-day delivery promise. The weakness is that carriage is a real cost that would further squeeze the $37.00 contribution, and it does not by itself encourage a second purchase.

Loyalty scheme: A points or repeat-purchase scheme directly targets repeat custom, rewarding the 49% of shoppers who would pay $20 more for custom-fitted frames and encouraging them to return. It builds a customer database for targeted marketing and, because rewards can be capped, the cost is more controllable than a blanket discount.

Recommendation: ZAE should choose the loyalty scheme. It is designed for repeat orders, fits the premium custom-fitted positioning that 49% of buyers value, and controls cost better than a discount that erodes $37.00 contribution. Free delivery is rejected as a costly short-term conversion tool that does not create loyalty; seasonal discounts are rejected because they damage margin when input costs are already rising 10.5%, and ZAE should track the 4.2% return rate to confirm the scheme is not encouraging more orders than the line can fit accurately.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the options with minimal application to ZAE.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of ZAE with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of ZAE with a well-justified recommendation explaining why discounts and free delivery are rejected.

questions.question_text: ZAE's lens-fitting defect rate has reached 4.2%. Explain two benefits for ZAE of using team working, supported by democratic leadership, to improve fitting quality.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Team working brings fitters, quality staff and online support together to identify the causes of the 4.2% defect rate, pooling different perspectives that a single worker would miss. Democratic leadership encourages open discussion, so staff feel able to report problems early, helping ZAE cut the 6.8% defect-related return rate of a year ago and protecting the $55.00 selling price from remake costs.

Point 2: Working in teams raises motivation and shared responsibility for quality, which suits the hierarchical structure by making the 50 employees jointly accountable for the new $960,000 lens-fitting line. Higher engagement reduces the risk of errors that push online returns up, supporting the 18,500-unit output target and improving the 4.3 out of 5 customer satisfaction score as fewer faulty frames are dispatched. Democratic leadership also gives fitters a say in how the new $960,000 line is organised, which raises commitment and helps sustain 370 units per worker.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual analysis linked to ZAE's defects, returns and customer satisfaction.

questions.question_text: ZAE wants to cut its 4.2% lens-fitting defect rate. Consider an individual accuracy bonus or a profit sharing scheme. Which should ZAE choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Individual accuracy bonus: Paying a bonus to fitters who achieve low defect rates gives a direct financial incentive to reduce the 4.2% error level and is easy to measure against inspection results. It rewards the individuals responsible and can quickly improve accuracy on the new $960,000 line. However, it may encourage staff to focus only on measured errors, hide mistakes, or avoid helping colleagues, which could damage the team working pilot and push the 6.8% return rate back up if quality problems move elsewhere.

Profit sharing: A share of company profits gives all 50 employees a stake in ZAE's overall performance, encouraging cooperation and care across fitting, packing and online service. It supports team working and the democratic leadership style, and rewards improvements that raise profit through fewer remakes and higher satisfaction of 4.3 out of 5. The drawback is the delay between effort and reward and the fact that profit depends on outside factors such as the 10.5% input-cost rise, so the link to reducing defects is weaker than a targeted bonus.

Decision: ZAE should choose the individual accuracy bonus, with profit sharing introduced later. The bonus acts directly on the 4.2% defect rate, the urgent problem, and is measurable against inspection data, whereas profit sharing is too diffuse to fix fitting errors quickly. Profit sharing is rejected as the main tool because profit is affected by the 10.5% cost rise; team working alone is rejected because it lacks the financial incentive needed to change behaviour on the line, so ZAE should review the 4.2% defect rate monthly against the 6.8% return figure of a year ago.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two motivators with limited application to ZAE.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both motivators in the context of ZAE.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both motivators with a well-justified decision covering measurement, teamwork and cost pressures.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how ZAE's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $222,000 ÷ ($55.00 − $18.00) = $222,000 ÷ $37.00 = 6,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 6,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $55.00 − $18.00 = $37.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $37.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways ZAE's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 6,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 18,500 units to confirm the eyewear range is strongly profitable, leaving a margin of safety of 12,500 units, which supports the $960,000 investment.
2. Use average total cost of $222,000 ÷ 18,500 units + $18.00 = $30.00 a unit to monitor the cost of the 4.2% defect rate, setting a target to reduce remakes and lower unit cost.
3. Use contribution per unit of $37.00 to evaluate the $20 premium sought by 49% of surveyed shoppers for custom-fitted frames, since each premium unit adds directly to profit on 18,500 sales.
4. Use labour productivity of 18,500 units ÷ 50 staff = 370 units per worker to benchmark the automated lens-fitting line against the 2.9% click-through and 4.3 satisfaction scores, checking that quality improvements are not slowing output.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 6,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $37.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 18,500-unit output; average total cost of $30.00 to track the 4.2% defect rate; contribution analysis of the $20 premium; and labour productivity of 370 units per worker.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate ZAE's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has ZAE's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.79 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.89 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.03 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.08 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $130,000 inventories + $85,000 trade receivables + $90,000 cash = $305,000; 2025 current assets = $145,000 + $90,000 + $105,000 = $340,000. The 2024 figure is $305,000 ÷ $170,000 = 1.79; the 2025 figure is $340,000 ÷ $180,000 = 1.89. Excluding stock, 2024 liquid assets are $85,000 + $90,000 = $175,000, giving $175,000 ÷ $170,000 = 1.03; 2025 liquid assets are $90,000 + $105,000 = $195,000, giving $195,000 ÷ $180,000 = 1.08.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved modestly. The 1.79 to 1.89 rise shows current assets cover short-term debts more comfortably, helped by cash rising from $90,000 to $105,000. The 1.03 to 1.08 improvement means ZAE can meet liabilities from liquid assets alone without selling inventory, a strong position while it repays a $360,000 loan and spends $960,000 on the lens-fitting line. Both measures exceed 1 in both years. Nevertheless, trade receivables rose from $85,000 to $90,000 and inventories from $130,000 to $145,000, and with a 4.2% defect rate some stock may be slow-moving, so asset quality should be watched as the business expands.

Conclusion: ZAE's financial position has improved. Both measures rose and both remain above 1, so short-term solvency is comfortable and does not depend on selling frames. The main residual risk is higher receivables and stock, so ZAE should keep credit control tight while funding the $960,000 programme from its $600,000 share issue.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and cash movements and a justified conclusion on whether ZAE's position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for ZAE of offering custom-fitted frames as promoted in its market research.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Custom-fitted frames match the 49% of 750 surveyed shoppers who would pay $20 more, allowing ZAE to command a premium over its $55.00 selling price and increase the $37.00 contribution per unit. The offer also uses the 63% who buy eyewear online and can reduce the 4.2% defect-related return rate, because better fit means fewer remakes and higher 4.3 out of 5 satisfaction, supporting the $960,000 automated fitting line.

Disadvantage: Custom fitting is more complex and costly than standard frames, potentially raising the $18.00 variable cost per unit and requiring extra skill from the workforce of 50 at a time when the 4.2% defect rate is already a problem. The insert does not give the size of the extra cost, so the $20 premium cannot be proven profitable; if fitters make more errors, returns could rise above 4.2% and the benefit of the premium would be lost. With the sector's 12% average online return rate, fit accuracy is commercially important, so a premium based on poor fitting would quickly destroy value.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to ZAE's survey, defects and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise from 4.25% to 5.0%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 10.5% rise in lens and frame input costs will affect ZAE. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If ZAE's $360,000 loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $360,000 = $2,700 a year (0.0075 × $360,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $222,000 a year, and if the loan is fixed-rate the increase is zero. Higher rates could also slow consumer spending on accessories, though that grew 3.3%, and make future finance dearer, but ZAE can largely remove this risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $13.60 per hour): With a workforce of 50, this rise feeds into the wage bill for fitting, packing and online support and is unavoidable. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no defensible annual total can be invented. The correct benchmark is the given productivity figure: 18,500 units ÷ 50 staff = 370 units per worker. If productivity holds at 370 units and the 4.2% defect rate falls, the rise is absorbable; otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $37.00 contribution per unit is reduced.

Lens and frame input inflation (10.5%): The insert does not break down the $18.00 variable cost, so only a bound can be calculated: if the whole variable cost rose 10.5%, that adds 10.5% × $18.00 = $1.89 per unit, or about $34,965 a year at 18,500 units. Even a smaller rise would erode contribution, and with accessory spending up only 3.3% and online returns averaging 12%, ZAE may find it hard to pass the cost on through its $55.00 price.

Conclusion: The 10.5% rise in lens and frame costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to all 18,500 units and directly threatens the $37.00 contribution that funds the $960,000 investment, and it is far larger than the $2,700 interest increment. The wage rise can be offset by 370-unit productivity and the interest rise neutralised by fixing the rate, so input inflation is clearly the dominant risk.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to ZAE.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on ZAE's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of ZAE with a well-justified judgment on which has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
